evidence: Cic. Flacc. 67: aurum … ex Ītaliā … Hierosolymam exportārī
Cic. Verr. 2.2.176: magnum numerum frūmentī … Syrācūsīs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To carry out, and so to send goods out of a country (Lewis & Short); it is also simply to carry something out of a house or a town.

evidence: Varr. RR 1.16.6: mercēs, opposed to invehere (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To carry out by cart or ship; Varro sets ēvehere and invehere side by side for what a farm sends out and brings in. Its other senses are to raise up (Hor. C. 1.1.6) and, in the passive, to ride or sail out.
Cicero’s noun, once (Lewis & Short), beside invectiō, import. The goods themselves are mercēs: exports, mercēs quae exportantur.

phrases.latin: Cum aurum Jūdaeōrum nōmine quotannīs ex Ītaliā et ex omnibus nostrīs prōvinciīs Hierosolymam exportārī solēret, Flaccus sānxit ēdictō nē ex Asiā exportārī licēret.
phrases.english: Since gold was regularly exported every year in the name of the Jews from Italy and all our provinces to Jerusalem, Flaccus forbade its export from Asia by edict.

phrases.latin: Jam vērō et eārum rērum quibus abundārēmus, exportātiō, et eārum quibus egērēmus invectiō certē nūlla esset, nisi iīs mūneribus hominēs fungerentur.
phrases.english: Again, there would certainly be no export of the things we have in plenty, and no import of those we lack, if people did not do this work.

sources: Lewis & Short: exporto · Lewis & Short: eveho · Lewis & Short: exportatio
